c43_pro_thinking_001.label: The Tyranny of Metrics
c43_pro_thinking_001.description: A pitfall where quantitative targets and KPIs distort behavior, leading to unintended negative consequences that undermine the original goals (also called 'Tyranny of Metrics').
coverage_criteria: Explain the concept of 'tyranny of metrics' with an example.
Identify a situation where a metric might cause goal displacement.
Propose a safeguard to prevent metric-induced behavior distortion.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article introduces this pitfall with a hospital readmission example and explains how metrics can displace performance, citing Kapoor (2018).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is specific enough to be checked with a few scenarios or explanations; it represents a distinct data-driven decision pitfall.

c43_pro_thinking_002.label: Misinterpreting Correlations as Causation
c43_pro_thinking_002.description: The error of assuming that a statistical correlation between two variables implies a cause-and-effect relationship, without considering confounding factors.
coverage_criteria: Define the difference between correlation and causation.
Provide an example where a correlation is mistakenly interpreted as causation.
Explain why rigorous causal analysis is important in data-driven decisions.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article explains this pitfall with a tech company example where demographic traits were wrongly inferred as causing productivity differences, and cites Gillespie & Patrick (2018).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is a fundamental statistical error often taught in analytics; it can be assessed with definitions and case applications.

Identify a scenario where overgeneralizing from a limited data set led to a mistake.
Describe how to supplement internal data with external perspectives.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article discusses this trap with a retail chain example and emphasizes that big data is still a sample, citing Davenport (2014) and Lee et al. (2019).

c43_pro_thinking_004.description: The tendency for data teams to only seek information that confirms their existing beliefs, creating an echo chamber that overlooks contradictory insights and black swan events.

Provide an example where a filter bubble led to flawed strategic planning.
Suggest a technique to counteract confirmation bias in data analysis.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article explicitly discusses this as a related trap to overgeneralizing, with an e-commerce strategic planning example, citing Pariser (2011).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept is a cognitive bias in data interpretation; it can be assessed by asking students to identify and counteract it.

c43_pro_thinking_005.label: Losing the Human Element in Data-Driven Decisions
c43_pro_thinking_005.description: The pitfall of overemphasizing quantitative data to the point where important human factors—such as skills, relationships, and cultural fit—are overlooked, as seen in AI-driven candidate screening.
coverage_criteria: Explain why data alone may fail to capture important human aspects of organizations.
Provide an example where an algorithm overlooked a qualified candidate due to a lack of demographic match.
Propose a method to blend quantitative data with qualitative human judgment.

extraction_reason.source_grounded_rationale: The article discusses this with a software startup example where an AI screening tool missed top talent, citing Pfeffer & Sutton (2006) and D'Aveni (2015).
extraction_reason.granularity_rationale: This concept highlights the limitations of purely data-driven approaches in human-centric contexts; it can be assessed with examples and mitigations.

c44_pro_thinking_006.label: Firm-Level Factors Influencing Intuition Use
c44_pro_thinking_006.description: Smaller firms allow more intuitive decision-making due to agility and less bureaucracy. Larger firms with heavy governance stifle intuition. Financial performance and slack resources affect reliance: poor performance may force intuitive decisions, while slack can either foster analytics or promote intuition (dissensus).

c44_pro_thinking_007.label: Team Power Structure and Psychological Safety as Moderators of Intuition
c44_pro_thinking_007.description: Centralized power (dominant CEO) enables one person's intuition to drive decisions, but may lead to unbridled intuition. Psychological safety encourages sharing and challenging intuitions, fostering effective team intuitive processes.

c44_pro_thinking_009.label: Causes of Intuitive Misses in Strategic Decisions
c44_pro_thinking_009.description: Intuition fails when there is excessive reliance without rational checking, dominant actor power centralization, lack of integration of diverse intuitions, or when applied to unfamiliar domains (e.g., new market entry without prior experience).

The student can explain why intuition is less reliable in new market entry decisions.

c44_pro_thinking_010.label: Practical Implications for Improving Intuitive Decision-Making
c44_pro_thinking_010.description: Organizations should develop intuitive awareness in business education, encourage executives to embrace intuition but be mindful of its boundaries, and foster expertise through deliberate practice, retention, and feedback to improve reliability.

c44_pro_thinking_011.label: Rational Decision-Making: Success and Failure Conditions
c44_pro_thinking_011.description: Rational processes excel in stable or hostile environments and when firms have resources for deep analysis. However, rationality can fail in dynamic environments, information overload, or when predicting human behavior, where intuition is needed.
coverage_criteria: The student can state when rational decision-making tends to be more effective (stable, hostile, resource-rich contexts).
The student can identify situations where excessive reliance on rationality leads to missed opportunities (dynamic environments, services, human behavior).
